titleText.es: Cuando salga Guitar Hero 2 tendré material conversacional durante MESES
titleText.en: When Guitar Hero 2 comes out I'll have conversational material for MONTHS.

applications.explanationEn: Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks what.

regions.labelEs: OH, MUCHA VARIEDAD. ALGO DE ROCK CLÁSICO COMO BOSTON, PERO TAMBIÉN POR SUPUESTO QUEEN Y BOWIE, JOAN JETT...

applications.explanationEn: Algo de introduces an unspecified amount before the music style that follows.
Por supuesto adds the speaker's emphatic sense that this choice is obvious.

regions.labelEs: DESDE LUEGO NECESITAMOS MÁS SONIDOS ASÍ.

applications.explanationEn: Desde luego works as one fixed expression of strong agreement here.

regions.labelEs: PERO TAMBIÉN HAY COSAS NUEVAS CHULAS, COMO FRANZ FERDINAND, THE DONNAS Y AUDIOSLAVE.
ALGUNAS VECES SON DEMASIADO PARA MÍ. ME VAN MÁS COSAS COMO ARCADE FIRE, O CON ALGUNOS SONIDOS ELECTRÓNICOS COMO EN POSTAL SERVICE.

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the person whose taste is described, while plural van agrees with the plural cosas that appeal. Más belongs to the particular thing-group in this occurrence.
Ya te digo is an emphatic conversational agreement here, not merely a report about speaking.

regions.labelEs: EL POP SINTÉTICO PUEDE SER DIVERTIDO, PERO ME PARECE QUE A VECES HAY QUE DAR CAÑA CON ALGO DE METALLICA.

applications.explanationEn: Parece que introduces the speaker's impression before the following idea.
A veces marks the claim as true on some occasions rather than always.
Hay que expresses general necessity, and dar remains in its unchanged dictionary form.
Dar caña is the informal fixed expression for adding forceful energy here; caña is not literal cane.
Algo de introduces an unspecified amount before the band name that follows.
The comic prints QUIENES without an accent. In standard spelling, a direct question uses quiénes with an accent.

regions.labelEs: PARECE QUE DOMINO DE MÚSICA HASTA QUE LA GENTE DESCUBRE QUE SOLO ESTOY ENUMERANDO GRUPOS DE GUITAR HERO.

applications.explanationEn: Parece que frames what follows as the speaker's impression.
The printed de tries to mark music as the topic. Standard Spanish would more naturally say domino la música or entiendo de música.
Hasta que introduces a recurring endpoint, and descubre stays in its ordinary present form because the discovery is presented as a repeated fact.
Estoy changes for the speaker, while enumerando is the -ando form that presents the listing as in progress.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.noteEn: Escuchar goes directly before what is heard. Spanish does not add a separate word for the English “to” in “listen to.”

example.en: I listen to music at home.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “some” or “a bit of” before a thing or substance?
cards.answerEn: Use algo de before the noun.
cards.noteEn: Algo stays unchanged, and de connects it to what the unspecified amount consists of.

cards.answerEn: a rhythm video game whose soundtrack supplies the bands named in the comic
cards.noteEn: Players perform rock songs with a guitar-shaped controller. The joke is that apparent music knowledge can come from memorizing the game's track list rather than exploring the artists independently.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “of course” when something is obvious or agreed?
cards.noteEn: Por supuesto is a fixed expression. It can confirm a request or emphasize that the speaker sees something as expected.

example.en: Of course, you can come in.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)
Joan (part of the name Joan Jett)
Jett (part of the name Joan Jett)
no separate English word; part of desde luego (“of course”)

cards.questionEn: How can desde luego show strong agreement or certainty?
cards.noteEn: Treat it as one fixed expression here; its meaning is not assembled from the usual separate meanings of desde and luego.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of desde luego (“of course”)
Franz (part of the band name Franz Ferdinand)
Ferdinand (part of the band name Franz Ferdinand)
The (part of the English band name The Donnas)
Donnas (part of the band name The Donnas)

cards.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.answerEn: me (after a preposition such as para)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).

cards.promptEs: irle algo a alguien, con sentido de gustos
cards.questionEn: How do you say that something suits someone or is their kind of thing?
cards.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before a form of ir that matches the thing that suits or appeals.
cards.noteEn: The short word identifies the person whose taste is described. The form of ir matches the thing that appeals, not that person: va for one thing and van for several things in the present; another time frame can use forms such as fue or fueron. Os identifies more than one person addressed informally in Spain. This preference use is especially common in informal Spanish in Spain.

example.en: Quiet films are my kind of thing.

cards.answerEn: Arcade (part of the band name Arcade Fire)
Fire (part of the band name Arcade Fire)
Postal (part of the band name Postal Service)
Service (part of the band name Postal Service)
indeed; adds emphatic agreement in ya te digo

cards.questionEn: What can ya te digo mean as a reaction in conversation?
cards.answerEn: It often means “Absolutely” or “Tell me about it,” showing strong agreement.
cards.noteEn: The literal pieces relate to “I already tell you,” but conversational ya te digo commonly reacts to what the other person has just said rather than announcing a new act of telling.
Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

cards.answerEn: do you know; are you familiar with
Parece que… means “It seems that…” or “It looks as though…”
cards.noteEn: Put a complete statement after que. Use this pattern when the available evidence points toward a conclusion, but you are not presenting that conclusion as completely certain.
cards.questionEn: How do you introduce something that seems likely but is not certain?

example.en: It looks like it is going to rain.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.

cards.answerEn: one must; it is necessary (as part of hay que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something has to be done without naming who must do it?
cards.answerEn: Use hay que followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Hay que does not change for a person; it gives a general requirement, like English “one must,” “you have to,” or “we need to.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links hay to the required action
to give; here part of dar caña (“go hard; turn up the intensity”)

cards.questionEn: What can dar caña mean in informal Spanish?
cards.answerEn: It can mean to go hard, push something, or turn up the intensity; the natural English wording depends on the situation.
cards.noteEn: This informal expression is common in Spain. Caña literally has other meanings, including “cane,” but those literal meanings do not explain the expression's energetic sense.

example.es: Vamos a dar caña en el entrenamiento.

cards.answerEn: intensity or energy (in the informal expression dar caña)
who? (plural; standard spelling in this question is quiénes)
cards.noteEn: The comic prints quienes without an accent. In a direct question, standard Spanish writes quiénes; it asks about more than one person.

cards.promptEs: hasta que + hecho habitual o conocido
cards.questionEn: What verb form follows hasta que for a usual or already-known event?
cards.answerEn: Use an ordinary statement form when the event is habitual, known, or already completed.
cards.noteEn: Hasta que means “until.” Spanish uses an ordinary statement form for an event treated as a fact. A still-awaited future event instead uses the special subjunctive form; for example, llega is an ordinary form, while llegue is the corresponding subjunctive form.

example.es: Siempre leo hasta que empieza la clase.
example.en: I always read until class starts.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.answerEn: Guitar (part of the video-game title Guitar Hero)
Hero (part of the video-game title Guitar Hero)
